narrative: Two straightforward how-to tickets nine months apart — a calculated-percentage question and a seat-deactivation billing check — both resolved within days. No friction, no repeat contact on either topic. Light, healthy usage with nothing for CS to act on.

An alert-threshold-reverting bug reported 19 December recurred a 'fourth time' on 1 January with an explicit request to escalate, then sat open for a week while the customer disabled alerts entirely because 'I can't trust them.' By February they are asking for API access specifically 'to avoid the issues we've had with the UI reverting settings' — a workaround built around a fault never confirmed fixed. Financial-monitoring alerts going untrusted is a real signal even though the other tickets (report locking, dashboard refresh, one-off export) closed cleanly.

Three separate production-impacting problems are open at once by the end of this history: bulk exports stuck in 'processing' for over 24 hours, API writes returning 500s on what the customer calls a production incident needing a response 'within the hour,' and alert delivery that was 'supposedly fixed' in February but is back up to 90-minute delays, with the account stating 'I've stopped relying on the alerts for anything time-sensitive.' The August alert ticket asks outright whether the delay 'is going to be a persistent limitation' — a customer testing whether the vendor can ever actually fix this, not just reporting a bug.

Four months of genuinely broken budget alerts (silent, then wrong threshold, then duplicating) were escalated formally in May because 'budget alerting is core to why finance uses this platform.' A relapse in August is met calmly, and the arc closes with real confirmation rather than a hopeful close: 'Thanks for finally getting to the bottom of the alerts issue,' plus a separate note that report totals have matched source data for 'two consecutive close cycles.' The five tickets since September are routine admin and dashboard requests with no complaint tone — a genuine recovery, not a lull before the next flare-up.

We are due to review our BI tooling ahead of next year's renewal, and Dashlume has come up again in those conversations, mostly on the strength of dashboard responsiveness.

narrative: Dashboard slowness reported in March was marked resolved, came back in June ('hasn't really gone away... feels worse than before'), and by October is still 'intermittent' after three separate write-ups — the account has quietly adapted by 'scheduling exports overnight and working from those instead of the live view' and explicitly says 'no need to prioritise.' Dashlume is named in three consecutive tickets, moving from a passing mention to being tied directly to next year's renewal decision. This is the low-volume, unfailingly polite pattern that precedes a quiet non-renewal: no anger, no escalation demand, just a fault that never got fixed and a competitor now sitting inside the renewal conversation.

Four routine-to-moderate tickets over five months resolve cleanly, including confirmation that the original KPI-alert setup question got sorted 'with help from support.' The account ends on its angriest note: a connector down for three weeks with 'two tickets, same questions, no fix' and a demand for 'someone with real authority,' resolved only after 18 days — the longest wait in the account's history. Nothing is currently open, but the trend toward longer waits and less patience is worth a check-in.

A MySQL connector timeout closed in March came back in June with the customer stating the root cause 'was apparently never properly fixed — we just had a period where it happened to work,' and asking to be escalated; that triggered a cascade of dashboard staleness and a direct request for 'a dedicated account contact' after 'multiple issues over several months.' Since August, scheduled exports have missed runs repeatedly across two separate tickets, the second noting 'the ticket I raised last month was closed but the problem clearly wasn't fixed,' with the account now stating it 'cannot rely on scheduled exports for our reporting pipeline.' Two distinct core-reliability threads remain open at the end, alongside a documented pattern of tickets being closed before the fault was actually gone.

A spell of API timeouts forced the team into a manual Excel workaround for one week's reporting, but the fix landed within days, and a later alert-digest group issue closed just as quickly. Three tickets, no repeat complaints, no lingering tone — ordinary friction that got handled.

Two administrative tickets nearly a year apart — an ownership transfer and an API key rotation question — both closed without incident. Sparse contact with no complaint content of any kind; nothing here points to risk.

Consistently appreciative tone throughout — 'really useful,' 'loving the export options,' 'nice touch' — with explicit thanks when a requested feature (per-rule alert recipients) shipped. One thread worth flagging for product rather than risk: the account is piloting an unnamed 'lightweight BI tool alongside Kataja for one team,' showing some appetite to diversify tooling. Otherwise this is an engaged, satisfied customer making feature requests, not weighing an exit.

Six tickets, all API and dashboard how-to questions building toward a wall-display kiosk setup, resolved within days each time. Purely constructive, exploratory usage with no faults reported — a customer building out more use cases for the product, not questioning it.

Four low-urgency tickets — a formula bug, bulk seat reassignment, an SFTP export request, and a rate-limit question — each resolved within a working week and each opened with phrasing like 'not urgent.' Routine account management with no signs of strain.

The highest-volume account in this batch — 29 tickets over a year, spanning nearly every module, almost all resolved within one to two days but recurring identically: exports 'blank AGAIN,' a scheduled export that 'never arrived... second time this's happened,' an alert threshold that 'reset itself... that's twice now,' and a seat-billing mismatch flagged as the 'third time... this year.' This is a heavily dependent, board-pack-and-month-end-critical account that stays highly engaged and keeps escalating rather than going quiet, but the fast fixes are not holding — the same fault classes keep recurring through October 2025 with no sign the underlying reliability problems are actually being solved.

Four tickets across ten months, each low-urgency ('not urgent,' 'when convenient') and resolved. The Fortnox connector needed attention twice with different symptoms, but neither ticket carries frustration and there is no sign the recurrence is being treated as a pattern by the customer. Ordinary maintenance-level contact.

Three well-spaced, unrelated tickets over nine months — an export timeout, an unexplained connector pause, and an API access request for an intern — all closed without complaint. Low volume here reflects genuine quiet, not resignation.

Eight minor tickets over nine months, mostly small bugs and feature questions raised in a mild, unhurried tone ('minor annoyance,' 'flagging in case'). One thread — dashboard load time climbing from a few seconds to 15-20 seconds — was never confirmed fixed in a later ticket, so it should be treated as still open, but nothing in the surrounding traffic suggests the account is troubled by it.

A scheduled-export column-order bug appeared in March, was flagged again in July as 'the same shift in the same three columns,' and that second ticket is the one that actually closed it — a genuine if slow-to-land fix rather than a cosmetic close. Tone stays even and patient throughout ('been meaning to raise this for a while'), with no urgency language and no repeat complaints after resolution.
Four configuration and permissions questions over three months, each resolved within a week. Nothing recurring, nothing urgent — standard onboarding-adjacent support traffic.

Alert reliability breaks down three separate times across five months: a missed threshold in October, then in February 'we have raised issues with alert reliability before... this pattern of inconsistency is not acceptable,' then a third relapse in March when a platform update reverted thresholds and recipient lists the customer had 'carefully tuned.' Scheduled exports fail on a similar cadence ('not sustainable' by the second occurrence), and a December multi-connector outage left a historical data gap that was never confirmed backfilled. The language moves from technical questions to explicit statements that patches are not holding, the clearest deterioration marker in this account.

A report builder crash ran unresolved for three months (October to January), losing work three separate times before an explicit escalation demanding 'a real fix or a real timeline'; seat provisioning was still broken and unaddressed as of March, with the customer asking for 'a call with someone who can actually own this.' The account then goes quiet for five months and returns in August with confirmation the export fix is 'holding up,' alerts are 'firing consistently again, which is a relief,' and by October is filing only low-priority feature requests 'while things have been running smoothly.' A genuine recovery arc — the escalation worked — though the March seat-provisioning complaint is never explicitly closed out in text.
